hip dysplasia.whatItIs: A malformation of the hip joint where the ball and socket do not fit together properly. The joint wears unevenly over time, leading to pain and arthritis.
hip dysplasia.whyItMatters: It is one of the most common inherited orthopaedic problems in dogs, and one of the most influenced by owner decisions: body weight and growth rate materially change how severe it becomes.

hip and elbow dysplasia.whatItIs: Malformation of the hip and elbow joints, where the bones do not fit together smoothly. Both joints wear unevenly and develop arthritis over time.
hip and elbow dysplasia.whyItMatters: Large and giant breeds are most affected. Screening schemes (OFA, PennHIP, BVA) grade breeding animals specifically to reduce it.

elbow dysplasia.whatItIs: A group of developmental abnormalities in the elbow joint that cause the joint surfaces to fit together imperfectly.
elbow dysplasia.whyItMatters: Often shows as front-limb lameness in young, growing dogs rather than in old age.

patellar luxation.whatItIs: The kneecap slips out of its groove, usually towards the inside of the leg. Graded 1 to 4 by how easily and how often it displaces.
patellar luxation.whyItMatters: Very common in toy and small breeds. Mild grades may need no treatment; higher grades cause arthritis and often need surgery.

gastric dilatation-volvulus.whatItIs: The stomach fills with gas and then twists on itself, cutting off its own blood supply. Also called bloat or GDV.
gastric dilatation-volvulus.whyItMatters: This is a true emergency. Without surgery within hours it is usually fatal. Deep-chested breeds are most at risk, and a preventive surgery (gastropexy) can be done during neutering.

hypothyroidism.whatItIs: The thyroid gland produces too little thyroid hormone, slowing the body's metabolism.
hypothyroidism.whyItMatters: Easily missed because the signs look like ordinary ageing. It is diagnosed with a blood test and managed well with daily medication.

progressive retinal atrophy.whatItIs: An inherited condition in which the light-sensing cells at the back of the eye gradually die, leading to blindness.
progressive retinal atrophy.whyItMatters: There is no treatment, but a DNA test exists for many breeds, so responsible breeding can eliminate it. Dogs adapt remarkably well to gradual vision loss.

ear infections.whatItIs: Inflammation and infection of the ear canal, usually bacterial or yeast, often triggered by moisture or allergies.
ear infections.whyItMatters: Breeds with heavy drop ears are most affected, and Singapore's humidity makes recurrence more likely. Repeated infections can permanently narrow the canal.

otitis externa.whatItIs: Inflammation of the external ear canal, the medical name for the common ear infection.
otitis externa.whyItMatters: Frequently a symptom of an underlying allergy rather than a standalone problem, so recurring cases deserve an allergy workup.

epilepsy.whatItIs: A neurological condition causing recurrent seizures with no other identifiable cause.
epilepsy.whyItMatters: Usually first appears between one and five years of age. Most dogs live a normal lifespan with medication. Keeping a written seizure diary genuinely helps the vet adjust treatment.

intervertebral disc disease.whatItIs: The cushioning discs between the spinal vertebrae bulge or rupture, pressing on the spinal cord.
intervertebral disc disease.whyItMatters: Long-backed and short-legged breeds are predisposed. Sudden hind-limb weakness or dragging is an emergency, since prompt surgery greatly improves the outcome.

brachycephalic obstructive airway syndro.whatItIs: Flat-faced breeds have soft tissue crowded into a shortened skull, narrowing the airway. Also called BOAS.
brachycephalic obstructive airway syndro.whyItMatters: In Singapore's heat and humidity this is the single most dangerous breed trait: affected dogs cannot cool themselves efficiently and can collapse from heatstroke on an ordinary walk.

brachycephalic airway compromise.whatItIs: Restricted airflow caused by the shortened skull shape of flat-faced breeds.
brachycephalic airway compromise.whyItMatters: Heat intolerance is the practical danger in tropical climates. Weight control and surgical correction of narrowed nostrils both help substantially.

tracheal collapse.whatItIs: The windpipe's cartilage rings weaken and flatten, narrowing the airway during breathing.
tracheal collapse.whyItMatters: Produces the characteristic goose-honk cough in toy breeds. Using a harness instead of a neck collar is the simplest and most effective thing an owner can do.

dental disease.whatItIs: Plaque hardens into tartar, inflaming the gums and eventually destroying the tissue and bone holding the teeth.
dental disease.whyItMatters: The most common disease in adult dogs and one of the most preventable. Small breeds suffer worst because their teeth are crowded.

obesity.whatItIs: Excess body fat, most simply assessed by whether you can feel the ribs and see a waist from above.
obesity.whyItMatters: It worsens nearly every other condition on this list, particularly joint disease and breathing problems, and shortens lifespan measurably.

glaucoma.whatItIs: Pressure builds inside the eye, damaging the optic nerve.
glaucoma.whyItMatters: A painful red eye with sudden vision change is an emergency: sight can be lost within a day or two without treatment.

cataracts.whatItIs: The lens of the eye becomes cloudy, blocking light from reaching the retina.
cataracts.whyItMatters: May be inherited or secondary to diabetes. Surgery can restore vision in suitable cases.

corneal ulcers.whatItIs: A wound or erosion on the clear surface of the eye.
corneal ulcers.whyItMatters: Breeds with prominent eyes are highly vulnerable. Any squinting deserves same-day attention, because an untreated ulcer can perforate the eye.

entropion.whatItIs: The eyelid rolls inward so the eyelashes rub against the surface of the eye.
entropion.whyItMatters: Constant irritation causes ulcers and scarring. Surgical correction is straightforward and permanent.

dilated cardiomyopathy.whatItIs: The heart muscle thins and stretches, so the heart pumps less effectively.
dilated cardiomyopathy.whyItMatters: Often silent until quite advanced, which is why at-risk breeds are screened with echocardiography before symptoms appear.

mitral valve disease.whatItIs: The valve between the left heart chambers thickens and leaks, so blood flows backwards with each beat.
mitral valve disease.whyItMatters: Extremely common in older small breeds. Counting your dog's resting breathing rate at home is a simple way to spot early deterioration.

osteosarcoma.whatItIs: An aggressive cancer of the bone, most often in the limbs of large and giant breeds.
osteosarcoma.whyItMatters: Frequently mistaken for a sprain at first. Any limp in a large-breed dog that does not resolve within a couple of weeks deserves an X-ray.

legg-calve-perthes disease.whatItIs: The blood supply to the head of the femur fails, causing the bone to break down inside the hip joint.
legg-calve-perthes disease.whyItMatters: Affects small breeds in puppyhood, typically between five and eight months. Surgery usually gives an excellent outcome.

anaesthetic sensitivity.whatItIs: Sighthounds metabolise certain anaesthetic drugs differently because of their low body fat and distinct liver enzymes.
anaesthetic sensitivity.whyItMatters: Not a disease, but critical safety information. Tell every veterinary clinic your dog is a sighthound before any procedure, including dental cleaning.

deafness.whatItIs: Partial or complete hearing loss, often congenital and linked to coat colour patterns such as merle or piebald.
deafness.whyItMatters: Confirmed with a BAER test. Deaf dogs live full lives but need hand-signal training and must never be off-leash near traffic.

diabetes mellitus.whatItIs: The body cannot regulate blood sugar, either through insufficient insulin or poor response to it.
diabetes mellitus.whyItMatters: Increased drinking and urination with weight loss are the classic early signs. Managed with daily insulin and consistent feeding.

allergic skin disease.whatItIs: An overreaction of the immune system to environmental or food triggers, showing up in the skin rather than the nose.
allergic skin disease.whyItMatters: Paw licking and recurring ear infections are the usual first signs. Humid climates worsen flare-ups year-round rather than seasonally.

skin fold dermatitis.whatItIs: Infection in the warm, moist skin folds of wrinkled breeds.
skin fold dermatitis.whyItMatters: Almost entirely preventable with a few minutes of routine cleaning and thorough drying several times a week.

cushings disease.whatItIs: The body produces too much cortisol, usually because of a small benign tumour on the pituitary or adrenal gland.
cushings disease.whyItMatters: Signs are easy to dismiss as ageing: drinking more, a pot-bellied appearance, and thinning coat. It is treatable with medication.

von willebrands disease.whatItIs: An inherited clotting disorder in which the blood lacks a protein needed to stop bleeding.
von willebrands disease.whyItMatters: Usually silent until injury or surgery. A DNA test result on file before any procedure can prevent a serious bleeding event.

degenerative myelopathy.whatItIs: A progressive disease of the spinal cord that causes gradual hind-limb weakness in older dogs. It is not painful.
degenerative myelopathy.whyItMatters: A DNA test identifies at-risk dogs. There is no cure, but physiotherapy and mobility aids maintain quality of life for a long time.

exercise-induced collapse.whatItIs: An inherited condition where intense exercise triggers hind-limb weakness and collapse, with recovery after rest.
exercise-induced collapse.whyItMatters: A DNA test exists. Affected dogs live normally when high-intensity activity is managed.

parasites.whatItIs: Internal and external parasites including heartworm, ticks, fleas and intestinal worms.
parasites.whyItMatters: In tropical climates parasite pressure is year-round rather than seasonal, so preventives should never be paused over a 'cold season'.

periodontal disease.whatItIs: Inflammation and destruction of the tissues supporting the teeth, caused by long-term plaque and tartar.
periodontal disease.whyItMatters: Painful and very common, yet largely preventable with daily brushing. Bacteria from diseased gums can also affect the heart and kidneys.

skin allergies.whatItIs: An overreaction to environmental or food allergens that shows up as itchy, inflamed skin.
skin allergies.whyItMatters: Paw licking and repeated ear infections are usually the first sign. Humid climates cause year-round rather than seasonal flare-ups.

atopic dermatitis.whatItIs: A lifelong allergic skin condition triggered by environmental allergens such as dust mites, pollens and moulds.
atopic dermatitis.whyItMatters: Manageable but not curable. Early identification of triggers reduces the number of secondary skin and ear infections.

cruciate ligament rupture.whatItIs: Tearing of the ligament that stabilises the knee joint, usually from gradual degeneration rather than a single injury.
cruciate ligament rupture.whyItMatters: One of the most common orthopaedic surgeries in dogs. Keeping the dog lean substantially reduces the risk, including in the opposite knee.

fanconi syndrome.whatItIs: The kidney tubules fail to reabsorb nutrients, so glucose, protein and electrolytes are lost in the urine.
fanconi syndrome.whyItMatters: Manageable for years with a strict supplementation protocol, but only if caught early — which is why at-risk breeds have urine monitored from young adulthood.

collie eye anomaly.whatItIs: An inherited malformation of the tissues at the back of the eye, present from birth.
collie eye anomaly.whyItMatters: Mild cases cause no visible problem and are found only on an eye exam, which is exactly why breeding stock must be DNA tested and screened.

aortic stenosis.whatItIs: A narrowing below the aortic valve that forces the heart to work harder to pump blood out.
aortic stenosis.whyItMatters: Often detected as a heart murmur in a young dog. Severity varies widely, so specialist cardiac assessment matters before assuming it is harmless.

subvalvular aortic stenosis.whatItIs: A narrowing just below the aortic valve, restricting blood flow leaving the heart.
subvalvular aortic stenosis.whyItMatters: Usually found as a murmur in puppies. Severe cases can cause fainting or sudden death, so it should never be dismissed without an echocardiogram.

portosystemic shunt.whatItIs: An abnormal blood vessel that lets blood bypass the liver, so toxins are not filtered out.
portosystemic shunt.whyItMatters: Typically seen in poorly growing puppies who seem disoriented after meals. Often correctable with surgery.

lens luxation.whatItIs: The lens slips out of position inside the eye, often blocking fluid drainage.
lens luxation.whyItMatters: A painful red eye with sudden vision change is an emergency; rapid treatment can save the eye.

cancer.whatItIs: Uncontrolled growth of abnormal cells, which may form lumps or affect internal organs.
cancer.whyItMatters: Some breeds carry markedly elevated risk. Having every new lump checked promptly, rather than watching it, is the single most useful owner habit.

hereditary cataracts.whatItIs: Clouding of the lens caused by an inherited gene rather than age or diabetes.
hereditary cataracts.whyItMatters: DNA tests exist for several breeds. Surgery can restore vision in suitable cases.

hyperlipidaemia.whatItIs: Persistently high levels of fat in the blood, which can inflame the pancreas.
hyperlipidaemia.whyItMatters: Diet discipline genuinely matters here — a single fatty treat can trigger a painful bout of pancreatitis in predisposed breeds.

urinary stones.whatItIs: Mineral crystals that form stones in the bladder or urinary tract.
urinary stones.whyItMatters: Straining to urinate in a male dog is an emergency, because a stone can block the urethra completely.

protein-losing nephropathy.whatItIs: The kidneys leak protein into the urine because their filtering membranes are damaged.
protein-losing nephropathy.whyItMatters: Silent in early stages, so at-risk breeds are screened with an annual urine protein test rather than waiting for symptoms.

cervical vertebral instability.whatItIs: Compression of the spinal cord in the neck, also called wobbler syndrome.
cervical vertebral instability.whyItMatters: Causes an unsteady, scuffing gait in large breeds. A neck-neutral harness rather than a collar reduces further strain.

addisons disease.whatItIs: The adrenal glands produce too little cortisol and aldosterone.
addisons disease.whyItMatters: Called the great pretender because signs are vague and intermittent until a sudden crisis. A blood test rules it in or out cheaply.

mdr1 drug sensitivity.whatItIs: A genetic variant that prevents certain drugs from being pumped out of the brain, causing severe reactions to ordinary doses.
mdr1 drug sensitivity.whyItMatters: Not a disease but critical safety information. The DNA test result should be recorded at every clinic your dog visits.

copper toxicosis.whatItIs: Copper accumulates in the liver because the body cannot excrete it normally, gradually damaging liver tissue.
copper toxicosis.whyItMatters: A DNA test identifies affected dogs, and a copper-restricted diet started early prevents most of the damage.
